source_file: Berlin 2026 edition for next app devCon 2026 (flutterCon Berlin), sources listed on the page
question: Q6: Your Next Move

sections.prompt: Raise your hand if you deliberately learned something outside Flutter this year: native, backend, AI, product, people.
sections.hint: METR, Jul 2025: experienced developers were 19% slower with AI tools while believing they were faster. Ask what they learned that an agent could not learn for them.
no_hands: What is the deep skill you are protecting, and is it safe from AI?
What would you learn next if you had one free day a week?
For the seniors: which skill paid off the most over your career, and was it technical?
hands_up: What did you learn, and did it change what work comes to you?
Did you learn it with AI, and did that help or make it shallow?
Was it depth, like native internals or architecture, or breadth, like product, people, business?
How do you show that learning to an employer or a client?
follow_ups: What should a Flutter developer deliberately still do by hand in the next year?
Which skill pairing with Flutter is underrated right now?

sections.model: An App With Your Name On It
sections.prompt: Raise your hand if you have an app in a store or on the web right now that you built yourself.
sections.hint: Google Play: a new personal developer account needs a closed test with 12 testers for 14 days before production. Ask what shipping taught them that tutorials did not.
no_hands: What stopped you: an idea, time, store hurdles, or no need?
Would a shipped app help you more than a certificate or a course?
For hirers: does a shipped app with real users change how you read a candidate?
hands_up: What did shipping teach you that no tutorial did?
Real users, real money, real support requests: which of those do you have?
Did it lead to anything: a job, a client, a talk, a lesson?
How much of it would you let an agent build today, and what would you keep by hand?
follow_ups: What is the smallest app that would prove serious ability in one weekend?
What would you build to show product judgment rather than code generation?

sections.prompt: Raise your hand if you have turned down a job or a project this year because of its tech stack.
sections.hint: JetBrains DevEco 2025: 68% of developers expect employers to require AI proficiency. Ask whether the no was about the stack or about how the company decides.
no_hands: What would you say yes to even if it were not Flutter: the product, the team, the pay?
How much does the framework matter next to the domain and the people?
For juniors: can you afford to say no right now, and who told you that you cannot?
hands_up: What was the stack, and what was the real reason: technology, team, or the AI expectations?
What questions do you ask before joining a team now that you did not ask two years ago?
Was it a red flag about the stack or about how the company makes decisions?
Have you regretted a no, or a yes?
follow_ups: What interview question reveals whether a team uses AI to grow people or to avoid hiring?
Which opportunity would you take even if Flutter were not the main stack?

wrap_up: Hands up if you would still choose Flutter starting today. Compare with the worried count from Q1.
One sentence to your past self, from anyone who has been in Flutter for more than two years.
Where does this conversation continue: Flutter Berlin, Flutteristas, the Flutter Community AI Circle, or the native versus cross-platform panel on Friday?
